intent.task: Explain current-induced metal heating by charge-particle interactions and distinguish generated thermal energy from the conductor's retained internal-energy increase.
intent.source_solution: The electric field supplies energy to moving free electrons, whose interactions with material particles transfer electrically supplied energy into internal energy and can strengthen thermal motion. Charges do not vanish as fuel. Energy may then pass to the surroundings, so generated Q need not equal the conductor's net internal-energy increase. This is the stationary pure-resistor regime, not mechanical or chemical work.
intent.unit_reason: One native multiple response identifies the jointly necessary microscopic and energy-accounting distinctions. Options are assertions about one heating mechanism, not yes/no clicks for separate blanks or a combination-code answer.
limitations: Selecting explanations does not demonstrate independently composing the original written explanation.
No heating experiment, particle observation, or practical conductor operation is performed or verified.

rationales.derivation: Electric-field work supplies carrier energy; carrier interactions transfer it to the conductor's internal degrees of freedom. Strengthened thermal motion accounts for possible warming of the metal.

The candidate takes the fact that moving electrons can transfer energy to thermal motion, replaces the causal relation with identity, and concludes that directed drift is the same as random thermal motion. A preferred drift direction and random thermal motion are distinct.
rationales.misconception: Replace 'directed motion supplies energy to thermal motion' with 'directed motion is thermal motion', dropping the distinction between ordered transport and random microscopic motion.

rationales.derivation: For a conductor releasing energy outward, its net internal-energy increase is generated electrical heat minus energy passed to its surroundings. Hence the two quantities need not be equal.

The candidate assigns charge the role of combustible fuel: it treats outgoing current as consumed electrons, converts the supposedly missing charge into heat, then omits electric-field work. Charges carry energy and are not consumed in resistive heating.
rationales.misconception: Confuse consumption of electrical energy with destruction of the charge carriers and infer heating from charge disappearance.

intent.task: Determine generated heat from constant U,I,t in a stationary pure resistor; independently derive the current-resistance expression with Ohm's law; state the Joule-Lenz proportionalities and their held-fixed variables.
intent.source_solution: Pure-resistor electrical work becomes generated heat: Q=A=UIt. Ohm's law U=IR gives Q=(IR)It=I^2Rt, retaining both factors of I. With volts, amperes, ohms and seconds, both expressions yield joules. Compare I with R,t fixed to obtain square dependence, R with I,t fixed to obtain direct dependence, and t with I,R fixed to obtain direct dependence. Fixed voltage does not substitute for fixed current: at fixed U,t, Q=U^2t/R. I and R must remain constant or approximately constant through each full timed interval; temperature-dependent R requires care.
intent.unit_reason: Tasks 2, 3 and 4 form one coherent derivation-and-law argument, so a single complete report is the response unit. Every candidate carries the starting formula, substitution, simplification and all three controlled comparisons. Splitting into formula, exponent or per-variable clicks would fragment that argument and repeat its answer elsewhere.
limitations: Recognition of a complete report does not demonstrate independently writing the heat formula.
Recognition of the substituted expression does not demonstrate independently producing and organizing the derivation requested by task 3.
Choosing the complete law statement does not demonstrate independently verbalizing the law and its controlled comparisons.

rationales.derivation: Start from Q=UIt and U=IR, then collapse (IR)I into IR instead of I^2R. The resulting IRt predicts direct dependence on I, which reproduces the displayed linear-current claim and also loses the energy dimension.
rationales.misconception: Drop the pre-existing current factor after substitution, treating I multiplied by I as I rather than I squared.

rationales.derivation: Q=A=UIt in the pure-resistor regime. Substituting U=IR retains two current factors and gives I^2Rt. Dividing two runs with R,t fixed leaves the square of the current ratio; with I,t fixed it leaves the resistance ratio; with I,R fixed it leaves the time ratio. The declared SI units yield joules.

The algebra is valid, but the candidate reads the R factor in I^2Rt while substituting 'fixed U' for 'fixed I'. At fixed U, doubling R halves I; the product I^2R then halves rather than doubles. The claimed direct R proportionality under fixed U,t is therefore false.
rationales.misconception: Hold voltage instead of current fixed while reading a proportionality from a formula containing current.

rationales.derivation: Invert the resistance operation in U=IR to write U=I/R, then substitute into UIt. This mechanically yields I^2t/R and the claimed inverse resistance dependence at fixed I,t, but the substituted Ohm's-law relation and resulting heat law are invalid.
rationales.misconception: Rearrange Ohm's law by division instead of multiplication when expressing voltage through current and resistance.

intent.task: Calculate the full 30-minute generated heat from 20 ohms and 5 amperes under constant current and resistance, using consistent time and energy units.
intent.source_solution: t=30*60=1800 s. I^2R=5^2*20=500 W. Q=500*1800=900000 J. This is generated energy, not a temperature rise or just power. No numerical material data or calorie conversion is needed.
intent.unit_reason: One complete energy result retains squaring current, incorporating resistance, converting the whole duration and identifying joules. These steps belong to one calculation rather than separate arithmetic or unit-conversion clicks.
limitations: Selecting the completed energy result does not demonstrate independently writing the calculation, unit conversion or dimensional reasoning.

rationales.derivation: Compute 5^2*20=500 correctly but use the printed 30 as seconds: 500*30=15000, then label the result J.
rationales.misconception: Insert minutes directly into the SI-time formula without multiplying by 60.

rationales.derivation: Convert t to 1800 s but use IRt instead of I^2Rt: 5*20*1800=180000, then report that number as joules.
rationales.misconception: Use one current factor rather than its square while retaining the correctly converted interval.

rationales.derivation: Compute I^2R=5^2*20=500, stop before multiplying by 1800 s, and relabel the power's numeric value as total energy in J.
rationales.misconception: Confuse generated power with energy generated over the full interval.

rationales.derivation: 30 min=1800 s; Q=5^2*20*1800=900000 J. Constant I and R justify the full-interval product.

intent.task: Explain the purpose and physical basis of making a sound wire joint, using the source's soldering example only as principle analysis and preserving its prohibition on learner circuit work.
intent.source_solution: A poor joint can have large or unstable contact resistance. At the same current, local generated power is I^2 R_contact, so a sound joint that reduces and stabilizes R_contact reduces local overheating and intermittent-contact risk. The comparison is local and same-current; changing a whole circuit's resistance need not leave its current fixed. No soldering, supply-circuit assembly or disassembly is performed.
intent.unit_reason: One complete purpose-plus-causal-basis judgment tests the connection between contact quality and local heating. It is not a separate click for 'solder' or 'resistance', and the same-current qualification prevents an unsupported whole-circuit inference.
limitations: Choosing a purpose-and-basis explanation does not demonstrate independently writing the original explanation.
No practical connection, soldering, supply-circuit work, or verification of construction safety is attempted; the source restricts this task to principle analysis.

rationales.derivation: Treat a joint as a protective sacrificial load: deliberately raise its contact resistance to consume more energy there. At the stipulated same current this raises local power, which increases rather than prevents the joint's overheating.
rationales.misconception: Equate dissipating more energy at a contact with protecting that same contact from excessive heating.

rationales.derivation: Apply I=U/R with fixed U to claim that reducing contact resistance increases I, even though the stem fixes the compared current. At fixed I, reducing contact resistance reduces local generated power instead.
rationales.misconception: Import a fixed-voltage current change into a same-current local-contact comparison.

rationales.derivation: At common I, P_contact=I^2R_contact. Reducing and stabilizing R_contact lowers that local dissipation and a durable contact reduces intermittent connection, giving both the purpose and its physical basis without authorizing circuit work.

Model only the uninterrupted wire as a resistor, omit the finite resistance of the contact from the heating calculation, and conclude that joint looseness cannot affect local heating. A poor contact's resistance is precisely a local heating contribution.
rationales.misconception: Exclude a wire contact from the resistive model because it is a connection rather than a separately labeled resistor.

intent.task: Explain possible rapid burnout of an immersion heater removed while energized, distinguishing continued energy input from reduced heat removal and respecting the no-live-fault-experiment boundary.
intent.source_solution: Still-connected resistive heating continues supplying energy. Water normally removes heat effectively; removal into air greatly reduces that cooling. If generated energy exceeds outgoing heat, internal energy accumulates and temperature can reach damaging values. The source asserts possible failure, not inevitable failure of every apparatus. Temperature-dependent resistance and power do not eliminate the energy-balance mechanism; neither an exactly fixed power nor a current surge is assumed. Disconnect first; no energized out-of-water experiment is performed.
intent.unit_reason: One complete causal energy-balance explanation is the response unit. Isolated clicks for 'water', 'current' or 'temperature' would miss the relation between generation and removal; the judgment preserves that relation without asking for a live fault.
limitations: Selecting a causal explanation does not demonstrate independently producing the original written fault analysis.
No live fault, energized out-of-water experiment, practical operation or safety demonstration is carried out or verified.

rationales.derivation: Electrical energy input can continue after removal, while effective cooling by surrounding water ceases. The positive difference between input and outgoing thermal energy raises retained internal energy and can cause damaging temperature.

Treat water as necessary for electrical heat generation, then reverse the already outgoing heat flow and assign all energy previously given to water back to the removed heater. Neither automatic cessation of resistive generation nor automatic return of that energy follows.
rationales.misconception: Conflate the heated water with the electrical energy source and reverse past heat transfer when water is removed.

rationales.derivation: Treat the water layer as thermal insulation, replace loss of water cooling with enhanced air cooling, and then attribute burnout to that enhanced removal. The relevant ordinary mechanism is reduced heat removal, not increased cooling.
rationales.misconception: Reverse the cooling roles of water and air and treat removing more energy as the cause of thermal accumulation.

rationales.derivation: Compute the amount electrically generated over a duration and identify it with the element's retained energy regardless of outgoing heat. This drops the heat-loss term and falsely predicts the same temperature history in water and air.
rationales.misconception: Infer temperature solely from duration of electrical heating and discard differences in heat transfer to the surroundings.

intent.task: Preserve the equal-length/equal-area series-material task while assessing its invariant dependence on actual working-temperature resistivity and the insufficiency of unspecified grades; keep the conditional teacher-only demonstration and safety restrictions.
intent.source_solution: Equal geometry gives R_j=rho_j(T_j)L/S. Series wires have common current, not common voltage drop. With nonzero constant/approximately constant current and actual resistances during the common interval, Q_j=I^2t(L/S)rho_j(T_j), so the largest actual working-temperature resistivity gives the largest heat. The source supplies no exact steel/alloy grades, temperatures or resistivities; a universal named-material winner cannot be derived. That exact-ranking part is deferred rather than assigned invented rho values. If R changes substantially, Q_j is the common-interval integral of I(t)^2R_j(T_j(t)), not a product using an arbitrary initial R. Teacher-only suitable low-voltage demonstration remains an unperformed task; no household power or touching hot/energized wires is allowed.
intent.unit_reason: One native multiple response distinguishes the conditional physical ranking from missing material evidence and from series/parallel confusion. The unit is the complete comparative inference, not separate clicks for each material. The added visible constant/approximately-constant-resistance and working-temperature qualifications delimit the assessable invariant; they do not resolve the unavailable full transient or exact-grade ranking.

rationales.derivation: Under the visible nonzero-current, common-duration and constant/approximately-constant-resistance conditions, Q_j=I^2t(L/S)rho_j(T_j). The positive common multiplier preserves any strict actual working-temperature resistivity ordering.
